toc.title: Three reasons for the anxiety spike
It might mean you're safe enough to start

blocks.p: If meditation and breathing exercises make you more anxious, you're not broken. Your nervous system is potentially telling you something important. Let's break down why certain safety practices backfire, for freeze-dominant people in particular, what actually works instead, and what that post-practice anxiety spike really means about your recovery.

This comes from an email I got from someone I'll call Jeri, with an i. Jeri is working through Stuck Not Broken Book 2, which is about Polyvagal safety: how to access it and how to build it. Jeri writes:

"I believe I am mainly stuck in freeze and other times flight. In doing some of the safety anchors, I often then experience a huge amount of anxiety for a while. It's improved when moving away from stationary safety practices like breathing or meditation and doing things like mindful walking and/or movement. I will experience deep relaxation and then a while later, a huge physical anxiety. I believe this is a good sign, a sign of the body moving up the polyvagal ladder. I just wanted to check that I can expect this to reduce as time goes on. I'm in my second week of daily practice. I've also reduced the length of time I spend in safety anchoring. I was doing a lot, maybe 30, 45 minutes a day."
Thank you for the email, Jeri, and not only for reading Book 2, but for implementing its ideas and practices as well. There's a lot to get into with this question.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: We'll start with a potentially unhelpful assumption you may have. And this is for everyone, not just Jeri.

First off, in the Polyvagal Theory, safety refers to biology. There are specific biological pathways responsible for our capacity to think critically, to socially engage, to play, to create, and even to sit quietly in meditation.

Safety does not necessarily look calm, still, meditative, and quiet. It depends on what that biological pathway is mixing with. If you have safety plus the mobility of flight or fight, that combination results in play, productivity, creativity, and motivation. When safety combines with the immobility of shutdown, that results in stillness.

Freeze is a little different. Freeze is the combination of flight or fight mobility, the sympathetic mobility, plus shutdown immobility. It's mobile and immobile at the same time, like having one foot on the gas and one on the brake. This can be true for people who get triggered into a freeze, like a panic attack. But it can also be true for those who live in a chronic freeze, where their underlying state is freeze. That person is always in an underlying overwhelm, or panic, or rage.

So when people who are more flight, fight, or freeze dominated try to sit still and meditate, it doesn't go very well, because immobilizing, for them, is kind of not safe. Literally, in the environment, it might be safe. But as far as the body is concerned, in the nervous system world, there may not be safety internally.

Why would this be? Freeze is immobilization plus mobilization: feet on the gas and the brake. More immobilization, like meditation and breathwork, can feel like being trapped again. The internal flight or fight can't tolerate the immobility. And the immobility of freeze can't tolerate the internal unrest of flight or fight.

Freeze types often need to mobilize to cue safety. In fact, I think they're drawn to it. I've worked with freeze clients who feel a pull toward hyper-productivity, hyper-exercising, hyper-everything. Their body knows something their conscious brain doesn't: that movement is good. But the movement is out of control. Dysregulated. As their safety state strengthens over time, the dysregulated mobility decreases in intensity.

So needing movement is not a flaw. It's okay to need movement and to not feel okay with stillness practices. If you've ever felt like meditation makes you more anxious, or breathing exercises make you feel more trapped, or you need to move to feel better: yeah. That's okay. Your body's probably telling you something.

So instead of immobility, you might need movement. What kind of movement? I can't answer that for you in particular. I don't think that's the way this works. Some practical examples include walking, fidgeting, swaying, or even working out.

But no matter what movement you try, do it mindfully. Actually pay attention to the sensory input around you on a walk. Actually pay attention to your muscles contracting and stretching when you work out. As you bring a bit more mindfulness, also be a bit more aware of your breath. Not controlling it, just being aware of it.

As you do these, you'll probably slow down a little, and your connection with the present moment might increase. If you can do that, you'll be better able to connect with what's happening internally, and to let autonomic shifts happen spontaneously.

blocks.h: Three reasons for the anxiety spike

blocks.p: Now let's talk about the anxiety spike. When you anchor into safety through the ideas and skills in Book 2, there's a potential for defensive activation to surface during your practice, or even later on. This is a very normal and expected outcome of practicing safety. There are three possibilities I can think of.

The first possibility is that the body attempts to self-regulate while you do your safety practice, and when it does, the feelings of that state surface. For example, when someone in shutdown mindfully connects with their passive safety environment, they're likely to feel sadness. The sadness is already there, but now they're practicing present-moment mindfulness, so they're more aware of it. The body is also now accessing safety and naturally attempting to self-regulate, which is good, but it may be unexpected.

The second possibility is that the anxiety is an aftereffect of safety practices. In Book 2, the focus is on building safety and capacity, but it's not all hunky-dory. The body is undergoing autonomic shifts, so it needs to integrate and adjust. That's the best way I can put it. We may notice emotional shifts later on. I recommend to my clients that they don't push it, and do very minimal self-care for the rest of the day: enough water, rest, connection with other people, or maybe their pet. Basically, give the body a chance to recover from the autonomic shifts it's undergoing.

The third possibility is that the immobilization piece of the freeze is releasing, opening up the potential for movement, but the system lacks a sufficient vagal brake, which is the influence of the safety state on the heart.

You increase vagal brake strength by exercising the safety pathways. When it's sufficiently strengthened, the safety state's vagal brake calms the heart. And if the heart rate calms, flight or fight calms along with it.

So although safety is very possible, even for those living in chronic freeze, it's also likely that whatever's frozen might mobilize, potentially even to the point of dysregulation if the safety state isn't strong enough. Someone who's starting to regulate out of a frozen fight will experience increased agitation, and potentially rage, depending on vagal brake strength. A frozen flight might show up as anxiety, but also as panic, again depending on vagal brake strength.

blocks.h: It might mean you're safe enough to start

blocks.p: If this is you, or has been you, there's a good chance you've given up and lost hope, or you were terrified of what you assumed you would find within, or what would happen. These are valid concerns.

You may think, "This practice is making me worse." But the reality might be, "My system's finally safe enough to start processing, or to start self-regulating." You can reframe this as the beginning of unstucking. And yeah, it's not easy. I'm not saying that.

Think of it like starting a new workout routine. You might have moments when you feel incredible and motivated. You put in the reps at the gym, get your heart rate up, and sweat buckets. You feel proud and accomplished, and that's great. Good for you. But it's not all feeling empowered and motivated, right? Over the next day or two, your body recovers, but you may feel incredibly sore and achy. It might even hurt to move.

It's not exactly the same, but there's a parallel to the unstucking work we're doing here. As with that scenario, if you go too hard, your body will pay the price, and the recovery will be a struggle, no matter what stuck state you're in.
So I recommend working within your capacity. This is something I've really been harping on recently. Work within your capacity.

Working within your capacity means practicing the unstucking skills at a doable but challenging pace and depth. Person A might practice 30 seconds of simple mindfulness daily, and that's the best they can do. Person B might do a five-minute guided meditation a few times a week. Person C might practice self-guided meditation for 20 minutes a week, and every other day do simple sensory mindfulness practices.
There's no right answer. You need to listen to your capacity.

Once you get to the edge of what you can tolerate, it's probably time to compassionately greet that edge, and then stop the practice. You'll know you're at the edge of your capacity because uninvited and uncomfortable emotions and thoughts will show up, like fear or a painful memory. Those are clear signs.

We don't want to avoid these things. That's not the point. We want to invite them from a regulated state. When you're regulated, you can invite uncomfortable emotions and memories and thoughts with compassion and curiosity. But you have to be regulated.

So yes, the anxiety spike for someone coming out of a flight-flavored freeze is pretty darn normal, or at least a potential. Those spikes will come and go, and over time their intensity, frequency, and duration will decrease as you strengthen your safety state.
In the meantime, listen to your capacity. If the anxiety isn't improving, you're likely doing too much and need to scale back. Shorten your practices and simplify them as much as possible.

Jeri is a couple of weeks into their practices. Absolutely amazing. Keep going. The safety state can strengthen over weeks, but I would expect more like months. How many months? I can't say for certain. There are a ton of variables that come into play. I recently returned to focusing on my own safety practices, and because I was tracking it, I noticed that my safety baseline had increased over the past few months.
Let me switch gears now to the overall picture. Yes, you want to get unstuck from freeze. You want more freedom, more calm, and more connection. Of course. And it's possible to get there.

But keep in mind that when you're working with any stuck defensive state, including freeze, the goal of practice is to build capacity. There is no fix, no hack, no shortcut. I know you know that, but we need to keep it at the forefront of our mind.

So when you practice, think of it like putting in the reps at the gym to build strength. Or think of it like practicing drawing a face over and over to get better at drawing portraits. As you put in reps at the gym, you gradually get stronger. As you practice drawing faces, your skill increases and you can draw better portraits.
It's not easy, and it takes time. It takes patience, which somebody in freeze may typically have very little of. But as you practice safety, patience will probably grow along with it.

Freeze can thaw quickly, so it's important to listen to the body's signals and adjust your practices. Ideally, freeze thaws slowly. As freeze thaws, we gently connect with the flight or fight underneath it, and then channel it through mindful movement. And then we repeat, slowly and gently releasing the frozen mobility a little bit at a time.

I love this process because it puts you in the position of being your own expert. I want you to eventually build your own self-regulation. I want you to be able to recognize what's too much or too little, and to make small adjustments here and there. Just experiment and see what works best for you.
This is kind of a lot, so here are a handful of key points:

ul: If meditation makes you more anxious, that's not a flaw in you. That's your nervous system asking for something different. Listen to it, trust it, and keep going. Meditation may be most challenging for somebody in freeze, so come back to it another day, when you're ready to.
Safety looks different for different nervous systems. The right practice is the one your body tells you works. You have to listen.

Post-anchor anxiety, movement-based anchoring, shorter sessions, self-correction: all of this is progress. If you're in freeze or flight, experiment with movement-based safety cueing. Notice what happens, and trust that.
